tagline: The skin is the body's first line of defense, and the nurse is often the first to see it fail.
overview: Tissue integrity means intact skin, mucous membranes, cornea, and subcutaneous tissue that can protect, sense, regulate temperature, and repair itself. This concept covers normal skin structure and function, how to assess skin across all skin tones, infectious, inflammatory, and neoplastic skin disorders, how wounds are classified and cared for in acute settings, the labs and nutrition that affect healing, nursing, collaborative, and pharmacologic therapies, and skin changes across the lifespan.

topics.title: Skin Structure & Function
topics.summary: The skin is the largest organ in the body. Its three layers work together to protect, sense, regulate temperature, remove wastes, and make vitamin D.

sections.heading: The integumentary system
sections.body: The integumentary system includes the skin, hair, nails, and glands. The skin is the largest organ, and it protects and maintains health. Tissue integrity is broader than skin alone: it means intact skin, mucous membranes, cornea, and subcutaneous tissue. Impaired tissue integrity is damage to the epidermis and/or dermis. It is influenced by internal factors (genetics, age, overall health) and external factors (activity, environment, injury). At-risk groups include older adults, clients with limited mobility, chronic illness, trauma, and invasive procedures.

sections.heading: Layers of the skin
bullets: Epidermis (outer layer). It is the barrier layer and has no blood vessels. Keratin makes it durable and water-resistant, and melanin protects against UV damage.
Dermis (middle layer, the “working layer”). It holds the blood vessels and nerve endings that support sensation, plus the sweat and oil (sebaceous) glands and hair follicles.

Subcutaneous tissue / hypodermis (innermost). Technically it is not skin, but it is vital for protection. It stores about half of the body's fat cells, insulates and cushions, and anchors the skin to underlying structures.

sections.heading: Functions of the skin
bullets: Protection against microorganisms and trauma. Intact skin also keeps body fluids in.
Sensation: touch, pain, pressure, and temperature.
Temperature regulation: blood vessels dilate to release heat and constrict to conserve it, and sweat glands cool the body by evaporation.
Removal of toxins through sweat.
Vitamin D synthesis from UV light. Less sun exposure, more melanin, and older age all reduce it.

sections.heading: Lifespan snapshot
sections.body: Infants have thinner skin that gives less protection. Adults have thicker, more hydrated skin. Older adults have thinner, less elastic skin.

table.caption: Skin layers at a glance
rows: Keratin (durable, water-resistant), melanin (UV protection); no blood vessels
An injury limited to the epidermis does not bleed
“Working layer”: vessels, nerve endings, sweat and oil glands, hair follicles
Damage here causes pain and bleeding; loss of sensation ↑ injury risk
Stores about half of the body's fat; insulates, cushions, anchors skin

pearls: Any break in the skin creates two immediate problems: a portal for infection and loss of fluid and heat.
The epidermis has no blood vessels. A wound that bleeds has reached at least the dermis.
When sensation is lost (for example, neuropathy), the client must replace feeling with looking: daily skin inspection and testing water temperature with a thermometer or an unaffected body part.
redFlags: Loss of skin over a large area. Watch for fluid loss, heat loss, and infection.

topics.title: Skin Assessment & Lesions
topics.summary: Accurate skin assessment across all skin tones depends on knowing where to look, how to palpate, and the right name for what you see.

sections.heading: General skin assessment
sections.body: Inspect in good (natural, if possible) light and compare both sides. Assess color, temperature, moisture, texture, edema, and lesions, and ask about itching, recent changes, sun exposure, new products, medications, and home remedies. Describe lesions by type, size, color, shape, distribution, and drainage.

sections.heading: Cultural considerations: assessing darker skin tones
sections.body: Skin color varies with melanin, which protects from UV damage, so assessment differs for light and dark skin tones. Rely on sites with little pigment and on palpation.
bullets: Pallor looks yellow-brown or ashen gray.
Cyanosis: check the nail beds, lips, and buccal mucosa.
Jaundice: check the palms and soles, not just the sclera.

Pressure injuries and inflammation are harder to detect. Look for darker, taut, shiny, or indurated areas. Check temperature, edema, and induration, and compare with nearby skin. Moistening the skin may help reveal changes.

After lesions heal, darker skin may show discoloration. It is also at risk for melasma (dark facial patches from sun). Some products (makeup, bleaching creams) can irritate the skin or interact with medications.

sections.heading: Classifying skin disorders
sections.body: Skin disorders are hard to classify because symptoms (itching, redness, inflammation) are often vague. Two common methods are acute vs chronic and by type: infectious, inflammatory, and neoplastic.
bullets: Acute disorders are short-term with situational causes (bacterial infections, dermatitis). Treatment reduces inflammation and avoids triggers.
Chronic disorders are long-term or lifelong, with genetic or unknown causes (pigment changes, genetic skin conditions, psoriasis). Treatment aims for remission, not cure.
The skin can also reflect systemic disease. For example, dry skin with hair loss suggests hypothyroidism, and pinpoint bleeding spots (petechiae) can reflect a clotting problem.

sections.heading: Skin lesions
sections.body: Primary lesions arise from previously normal skin: macules, papules, nodules, vesicles, pustules, bullae, and wheals. Secondary lesions develop from primary lesions or trauma: crusts, scales, scars, keloids, fissures, ulcers, and erosions.

table.caption: Primary and secondary skin lesions
rows: Flat, nonpalpable color change, less than 1 cm
Raised, firm, deeper, larger than a papule
Clear-fluid-filled; vesicle less than 1 cm, bulla more than 1 cm
Transient, irregular, raised, itchy, edematous area
Loss of epidermis only / deeper loss into dermis or below
Fibrous tissue replacing damaged skin / overgrown scar extending beyond the wound
Healed incision / keloid on an earlobe

pearls: In darker skin, you often can't “see” redness. Palpate for warmth, induration, and edema, and compare with adjacent skin.
Pallor → conjunctivae and mucosa; cyanosis → nail beds, lips, buccal mucosa; jaundice → palms and soles, not just the sclera.
Document lesions by type, size (mm or cm), color, shape, distribution, and drainage. “Rash on arm” is not an assessment.
redFlags: Ashen gray lips and mucosa with a rapid pulse or low BP point to poor perfusion or oxygenation. Act, don't just document.
Raised wheals with hoarseness, wheezing, or throat tightness mean the reaction is affecting the airway.

topics.title: Infectious Skin Disorders
topics.summary: Bacteria, viruses, fungi, and parasites cause skin infections. The nurse recognizes them, prevents their spread, and teaches.

sections.heading: Causes and key points
bullets: Bacteria and viruses are the most common causes.
Fungal infections are more dangerous in immunocompromised clients (for example, clients receiving chemotherapy or with HIV/AIDS).
HPV (the virus that causes warts) increases cancer risk.
Prevention for everyone: hand hygiene, proper hygiene and skin care, and not sharing personal items (combs, hats, towels).

sections.heading: Bacterial: impetigo
sections.body: A contagious superficial bacterial infection, common in children. Vesicles and pustules break open and form honey-colored crusts, often around the nose and mouth. It spreads by direct contact, so use contact precautions and hand hygiene, gently wash crusts off with soap and water before applying the prescribed antibiotic, keep nails short, and don't share towels. Children usually stay out of school or child care until 24 hours after treatment starts.

sections.heading: Viral: chickenpox (varicella) and warts
bullets: Chickenpox: itchy vesicles in crops, with lesions in different stages at the same time. It is highly contagious, so use airborne + contact precautions until all lesions are crusted; only staff with documented immunity should care for the client. Relieve itching (cool baths, short nails) and use acetaminophen, not aspirin, for fever in children (Reye syndrome).
Herpes simplex and herpes zoster are among the most common skin conditions in the U.S. Their vesicles can be tested with a Tzanck test.
Warts (HPV) are common in children and adolescents and spread by touch, including picking or biting them.

sections.heading: Fungal: tinea (athlete's foot, ringworm)
sections.body: Fungi thrive in warm, moist areas. Athlete's foot causes itching, scaling, and cracked (fissured) skin between the toes. Ringworm is a ring-shaped scaly patch with central clearing. Diagnose with a KOH prep. Teach the client to dry between the toes, wear clean cotton socks and shower shoes in public showers, use the full course of antifungal, and not share towels, combs, or hats.

sections.heading: Parasitic: lice and scabies
bullets: Lice: itching, with nits attached to hair shafts near the scalp. Treat with an OTC pediculicide used exactly as labeled (no conditioner right before), comb out nits with a fine-tooth comb, wash bedding and hats in hot water and dry on high heat (or bag items that can't be washed), recheck the hair, and don't share combs, brushes, or hats. Insecticide sprays are not needed.

Scabies (a mite): intense itching, often worse at night, with small burrows in the finger webs and wrists. It spreads by close contact, so use contact precautions, treat the client and close contacts at the same time, and wash recently used bedding and clothing in hot water (or bag it).

pearls: Chickenpox: airborne + contact until ALL lesions are crusted. Assign only staff with documented immunity.
No aspirin for children with chickenpox or other viral illnesses (Reye syndrome).
Fungal infections are more dangerous in immunocompromised clients.
Lice and scabies spread through shared items and close contact. Teach clients not to share combs, hats, or towels.
redFlags: Any skin infection with fever and rapidly spreading redness, swelling, or drainage
A fungal skin infection in an immunocompromised client

topics.title: Inflammatory Disorders & Allergy
topics.summary: Acne, eczema, burns, psoriasis, and dermatitis are inflammatory skin disorders. Many are itchy and visible, and they affect comfort, sleep, and self-image.

sections.heading: Contact dermatitis
bullets: Allergic contact dermatitis: an immune (delayed) reaction to an allergen the client has met before. The rash appears at the allergen site, may form vesicles or wheals, and is shaped like the item (a watchband, a jeans snap from nickel, streaks from poison ivy). Common allergens include metals, poison plants, latex, dyes, and perfumes. Confirm with patch testing.

Irritant contact dermatitis: direct damage from chemicals, soaps, or detergents. It is not immune-related, so it can occur on first exposure. The skin is red, dry, cracked, and burning where it was exposed.
Age considerations: infants have the strongest irritant response (for example, diaper dermatitis), adults have most allergic contact dermatitis, and older adults have slower, less intense reactions.
Care: identify and avoid the trigger, wash the skin after exposure, use cool compresses and moisturizers, and give prescribed topical corticosteroids and antihistamines for itching.

sections.heading: Atopic dermatitis (eczema)
sections.body: A chronic, relapsing, very itchy inflammation caused by a weak skin barrier that loses moisture. In darker skin it may look darker brown, purple, or gray rather than red. Care: short lukewarm baths, a mild fragrance-free cleanser, pat dry and apply a thick moisturizer right away, cotton clothing, short nails, and avoiding triggers such as wool, fragrance, and heat. Prescription topical medicines treat flares. Scratching can lead to infection.

sections.heading: Psoriasis
sections.body: A chronic immune-related disorder in which skin cells build up too quickly, forming well-defined red plaques with silvery-white scale, often on the elbows, knees, and scalp. In darker skin, plaques may look violet or dark brown with gray scale. There is no cure, so treatment (prescription topical and oral medicines) aims for remission. Teach the client to moisturize, avoid injuring or scratching the skin, and manage stress.

sections.heading: Acne
sections.body: Puberty hormones increase sebum and sweating, so clogged follicles and bacteria produce comedones, papules, and pustules. Acne affects about 50 million Americans each year, including about 85% of people aged 12–24. Teach the client to wash gently twice a day, not pick or squeeze, and use non-comedogenic products. Darker skin is prone to dark spots after acne heals, so early treatment matters.

No; can occur on first exposure

pearls: A rash in the exact shape of a watch, ring, or jeans button suggests allergic contact dermatitis.
Eczema: lukewarm bath, pat dry, moisturize right away.
Chronic disorders such as psoriasis are controlled (remission), not cured.
Poison ivy rash is not spread by blister fluid. Wash the plant oil off the skin, clothing, and tools.
redFlags: Hives with wheezing, hoarseness, or throat tightness after an allergen exposure (airway involvement)
Scratched eczema or dermatitis that becomes red, warm, swollen, or starts draining pus (secondary infection)

topics.title: Skin Cancer, Screening & Prevention
topics.summary: Skin cancer is the most common cancer in the U.S. Many skin disorders, including most skin cancer, can be prevented or caught early with simple measures.

sections.heading: Neoplastic (cancerous) disorders
bullets: Basal cell carcinoma: the most common type. Often a pearly or waxy bump on sun-exposed skin that may bleed or not heal. It grows slowly and rarely spreads.

Squamous cell carcinoma: a rough, scaly, crusted bump or sore on sun-exposed skin (face, lips, ears, hands). It can spread. Rough, scaly sun-damage patches (actinic keratoses) can become squamous cell carcinoma.

Malignant melanoma: the most serious type. It arises from pigment cells and can spread early. Teach the ABCDE warning signs: Asymmetry, irregular Border, varied Color, Diameter larger than about 6 mm, and Evolving (changing). Any changing mole should be checked, whatever its size.

sections.heading: Risk factors
bullets: Genetics and family history increase risk (for example, a parent with melanoma).
Lighter skin has a higher risk of UV damage, and blistering sunburns add risk. Clients with darker skin can still get skin cancer, so all clients are at risk regardless of skin tone.
Extrinsic aging from UV, smoking, pollution, and chemicals causes precancerous changes.
Some medications (steroids, antibiotics such as doxycycline, chemotherapy, antifungals) may thin the skin or increase sun sensitivity.

sections.heading: Health promotion and modifiable risk factors
bullets: Sun protection: sunscreen (broad-spectrum, SPF 30 or higher, reapplied about every 2 hours and after swimming or sweating), hats, protective clothing, and shade. Avoid tanning beds.
Keep skin clean, dry, and moisturized. Avoid excessive cleansing, which dries the skin, and use moisturizers regularly.
Cover and care for wounds to reduce infection risk.
Avoid irritants and allergens: chemicals, dyes, perfumes, poison plants, latex, and metals.
Don't share personal items such as combs and hats.

Special groups: children need proper diaper care with frequent changes; chronic illness (diabetes, HIV/AIDS, obesity, poor circulation) increases risk; poor nutrition causes skin changes and delayed healing.

sections.heading: Skin screenings
bullets: Self-examinations help clients learn what their normal skin looks like and recognize changes early. Focus on sun-exposed areas (face, neck, ears, scalp, arms, legs) and also check the trunk, chest, and feet. Use mirrors or a partner for hard-to-see areas.
Professional exams: a full skin inspection by a dermatologist or provider, which may include biopsy, cultures, or patch testing.

pearls: Basal cell carcinoma is the most common skin cancer. Melanoma is the most serious.
“E” (evolving) matters most: report any mole that is changing, even if it is small.
Sun protection is for every skin tone.
Clients on photosensitizing medicines (for example, doxycycline) need extra sun protection.
redFlags: A mole that is changing, bleeding, or meets the ABCDE criteria. Refer for evaluation and biopsy.
A sore or scaly, crusted spot that bleeds or doesn't heal

topics.title: Wound Types & Classification
topics.summary: Classifying a wound by cause, skin integrity, contamination, and depth predicts infection risk and shapes acute wound care.

sections.heading: Types of wounds
bullets: Intentional wounds are created for therapy: surgery, venipuncture.
Unintentional wounds are accidental: fractures, lacerations.
Closed wounds: the skin is intact but the tissue underneath is injured (contusion). They can still hide bleeding and swelling.
Open wounds: the skin or mucous membrane is broken, which gives microorganisms a way in.

sections.heading: Classification by contamination
bullets: Clean: closed, no infection, sterile environment maintained (for example, a hernia repair).
Clean-contaminated: a controlled surgical entry into the GI, GU, or respiratory tract (for example, an elective bowel or gallbladder surgery).
Contaminated: an open, fresh accidental wound, a major break in sterile technique, spillage from the GI tract, or inflammation present.
Dirty/Infected: purulent drainage, dead tissue, or a clinical infection already present (for example, an old traumatic wound with pus, or a ruptured appendix).

sections.heading: Classification by depth
bullets: Partial-thickness: loss of the epidermis and part of the dermis. Heals by regeneration, usually with little or no scar.
Full-thickness: loss of all skin layers, possibly extending to muscle or bone. Requires connective tissue repair and leaves a scar.

sections.heading: Wound care in acute settings
bullets: Control bleeding: after hand hygiene and gloves, apply firm direct pressure and elevate.
Prevent infection: once bleeding is controlled, clean with normal saline and cover with a dressing.
Manage pain and swelling: apply ice (wrapped in a cloth, not directly on the skin).
Assess for shock: rapid pulse, cool clammy skin, low BP, restlessness. Report these right away.
Treated wounds: at each dressing change, monitor healing and check for drainage, pain, and signs of infection (increasing redness, warmth, swelling, purulent drainage, odor, fever).

table.caption: Wound classification by contamination
rows: No GI, GU, or respiratory tract entered; no infection; sterile technique maintained
GI, GU, or respiratory tract entered under controlled conditions
Open, fresh accidental wound; major sterile break; spillage; inflammation
Purulent drainage, dead tissue, clinical infection present

pearls: Tract entered on purpose and under control = clean-contaminated. A fresh accident or spillage = contaminated. Pus or dead tissue already there = dirty/infected.
Pressure and elevation first. Clean and cover only after bleeding is controlled.
Partial-thickness wounds regenerate. Full-thickness wounds scar.
redFlags: Bleeding that soaks through dressings despite direct pressure, or signs of shock (rapid pulse, clammy skin, low BP)
A closed wound (contusion) with tense, enlarging swelling, especially in a client taking an anticoagulant

topics.title: Diagnostics, Labs & Nursing Care
topics.summary: The right test identifies the cause of a skin problem. Labs, nutrition, hygiene, and infection prevention decide whether tissue can heal.

sections.heading: Diagnostic tests
bullets: Skin biopsy: identifies whether a lesion is benign or cancerous. Afterward, keep the site clean and covered and watch for bleeding and signs of infection.
Cultures of tissue, drainage, exudate, or serum identify infection and guide antibiotic choice. Collect them before the first antibiotic dose when possible.
KOH prep: detects fungal infection (for example, tinea).
Tzanck test: tests viral lesions (vesicles from herpes viruses).
Wood lamp exam: an ultraviolet (black light) exam in a darkened room. Some fungal infections and pigment loss show up under the light. The skin should be free of lotions and makeup.
Immunofluorescence studies: detect antibodies in skin samples (used for some autoimmune skin diseases).

Allergy tests: scratch, intradermal, and patch tests. Patch tests (for contact allergy) stay on and dry for about 48 hours, and the skin is read again a few days later because the reaction is delayed.
Carrier studies: nasal cultures for clients with repeated infections, to see whether they carry the bacteria (for example, Staphylococcus aureus).

sections.heading: Laboratory data and wound healing
bullets: WBC ↓: poor infection defense and delayed healing. A low WBC can also hide the usual signs of infection.
Hemoglobin ↓: less oxygen delivered to the tissues.
Coagulation studies: prolonged times → excessive bleeding. Hypercoagulability → clotting and poor wound perfusion.
Albumin less than 3.5 g/dL: poor nutrition, ↑ risk of infection and delayed healing.
Wound cultures: confirm infection and guide antibiotic choice.
Chronic illness such as diabetes also slows healing, so high blood glucose in a client with a wound needs follow-up.

sections.heading: Independent nursing interventions
bullets: Goals: control disease, prevent infection, and promote healing.
Assess home remedies, because some may hinder healing.
Hygiene: adults bathe daily; children and older adults every other day. Avoid harsh soap and use mild or liquid cleansers. Moisturize after bathing.
Teach comfort and skin-protection strategies.

sections.heading: Infection prevention, exercise, and nutrition
bullets: Infection prevention: proper wound cleaning and dressing, hand hygiene before and after wound care, safe disposal of soiled dressings, and teaching the signs of infection (redness, swelling, drainage, necrosis).
Exercise promotes blood flow and helps prevent pressure injuries.

Nutrition supports healing: ↑ calories, protein, and vitamins A and C. Encourage whole grains, vegetables, citrus, dairy, and lean proteins. Offer small frequent meals or supplements if intake is poor, and consult the dietitian.

table.caption: Matching the test to the question
rows: Changing mole, pearly bump that bleeds

pearls: Albumin less than 3.5 g/dL = risk for infection and delayed healing.
Get the culture before the first antibiotic dose.
KOH = fungus. Tzanck = virus. Patch test = contact allergy. Biopsy = cancer.
Hand hygiene before AND after wound care, and dispose of soiled dressings safely.
redFlags: A client with a wound, albumin less than 3.5 g/dL, and poor intake needs a dietitian referral and a nutrition plan now.
Fever, spreading redness, purulent drainage, or new odor from a wound
Bleeding from a wound in a client with prolonged clotting times

topics.title: Pharmacologic & Collaborative Therapy
topics.summary: Skin care is a team effort. Most skin medicines are topical, and safe use depends on applying them correctly and watching for irritation and interactions.

sections.heading: Collaborative therapies
sections.body: An interprofessional team improves outcomes through better communication and fewer complications. Key members include nurses, UAPs, wound care nurses, case managers, health care providers, dermatologists, oncologists, and surgeons.

sections.heading: Pharmacologic therapy
bullets: OTC medicines treat minor acne, lice, and sunburn.

Benzoyl peroxide: the first-line acne treatment. It kills bacteria and unplugs ducts. Expect some dryness and peeling; start with a thin layer, use gently, and know that it can bleach towels, clothing, and hair.
Salicylic acid: exfoliates (removes dead skin cells) and reduces inflammation.

Prescription medicines (oral and topical) treat eczema, psoriasis, and dermatitis. Topical corticosteroids are common: apply a thin layer with gloves, don't cover with an occlusive dressing unless prescribed, and avoid stronger products on the face and skin folds. Long-term use can thin the skin.
Skin tone differences: darker skin is more prone to inflammation and may need combination therapy (for example, chemical peels, microdermabrasion).

sections.heading: Nonpharmacologic therapy
bullets: Proper wound care, dressing changes, and nutrition.
Burns: daily debridement and sterile dressings.
Pressure injuries: care varies by stage and facility protocol.
Severe wounds: negative pressure wound therapy (vacuum devices).

sections.heading: Complementary approaches
sections.body: Aloe vera, chamomile, and evening primrose oil may soothe irritation and promote healing, but the evidence is limited. Ask every client about them, and monitor for drug interactions and allergies. For example, evening primrose oil may add to the bleeding risk of anticoagulants, and a product that burns or stings should be stopped.

table.caption: Common skin therapies
rows: Kills bacteria, unplugs ducts; dryness expected; bleaches fabric
Use exactly as labeled; comb out nits; recheck hair
Thin layer; no occlusion unless ordered; report skin thinning
Aloe vera, chamomile, evening primrose oil
Limited evidence; check for allergies and drug interactions

pearls: Benzoyl peroxide kills bacteria and unplugs ducts. Salicylic acid exfoliates and reduces inflammation.
Topical corticosteroid: a thin layer only, and no occlusion unless ordered.
Always ask about complementary products. “Natural” does not mean free of interactions.
redFlags: Thin, shiny, easily bruised skin where a topical steroid has been used for a long time
A complementary product used together with an anticoagulant, or one that causes burning, rash, or swelling

topics.title: Tissue Integrity Across the Lifespan
topics.summary: Newborns, children, adolescents, pregnant clients, and older adults each have expected skin findings. The nurse knows which ones are normal and which need follow-up.

sections.heading: Newborns
bullets: Vernix caseosa is a white, cheesy coating that protects the skin. It doesn't need to be scrubbed off.
Thinner skin means more heat loss and a higher risk of absorbing products put on the skin, so use products sparingly.

Common, harmless findings: milia (tiny white bumps on the nose and chin), neonatal acne, erythema toxicum (blotchy red spots with small pale-yellow or white centers that come and go and fade on their own), and birthmarks (for example, blue-gray patches over the lower back and buttocks in darker-skinned infants, which should be documented so they aren't mistaken for bruises).

sections.heading: Children
sections.body: Children have a larger body surface area, so they lose more fluid and heat. Common infections are fungal (tinea), viral (warts, varicella), and parasitic (lice, scabies). Other conditions: fifth disease (bright red “slapped cheek” rash, then a lacy rash on the arms and legs), roseola (several days of high fever, then a rash as the fever breaks), and pityriasis rosea (one larger oval “herald patch,” then smaller oval patches on the trunk). Diaper care: change diapers often and keep the skin clean and dry.

sections.heading: Adolescents
sections.body: Puberty hormones increase sebum and sweating. Common disorders are acne, dermatitis, psoriasis, fungal infections, and warts. Skin problems strongly affect body image, so address feelings as well as treatment.

sections.heading: Pregnancy
sections.body: Common changes are hyperpigmentation (for example, a dark line down the abdomen and darker patches on the face), stretch marks, and pruritus (itching). Atopic eruption of pregnancy (AEP) is an itchy, eczema-like rash that resolves after delivery.

sections.heading: Older adults and the aging process
bullets: Intrinsic aging starts at about age 20: slower exfoliation, ↓ moisture, ↓ fat cells. In the 30s skin becomes dull and thin; in the 40s ↓ collagen causes wrinkles; after menopause, ↓ estrogen makes skin thinner and drier.
Extrinsic aging comes from UV, pollution, smoking, and chemicals and causes skin thickening, precancerous changes, and wrinkling.

Normal changes: thinner, less elastic skin; wrinkles and sagging; slower healing; ↓ sebaceous glands → dry skin; ↓ subcutaneous fat → less cushioning and poor temperature regulation; paler, translucent skin (fewer melanocytes); age spots; fragile vessels (senile purpura); fat loss in the face and hands with gain in the thighs and abdomen.
Functional changes: ↓ sensation, ↑ healing time, ↑ injury risk, ↓ temperature regulation.

Nursing care: bathe every other day with lukewarm water and a mild cleanser, pat dry, and moisturize; lift with a draw sheet rather than dragging; pad bed rails and wheelchair arms; avoid adhesive tape on fragile skin; long sleeves protect the arms.

pearls: Vernix, milia, neonatal acne, and erythema toxicum are expected newborn findings. Reassure the parents.
Newborn skin absorbs products easily and loses heat quickly.
Pregnancy: hyperpigmentation, stretch marks, and itching are common; AEP resolves after delivery.
Older adults: no hot water, no vigorous rubbing, no adhesive tape on fragile skin, and never drag the client up in bed.
redFlags: Bruises in different stages of healing in protected areas (inner arms, trunk) that don't match the history, at any age
A newborn or child whose rash comes with fever, poor feeding, or lethargy

flashcards.front: Which skin layer contains blood vessels, nerve endings, and sweat and oil glands?
flashcards.back: The dermis, the “working layer.” The epidermis has no blood vessels.

flashcards.front: Name five functions of the skin.
flashcards.back: Protection (microorganisms and trauma), sensation, temperature regulation, removing toxins through sweat, and vitamin D synthesis from UV light.

flashcards.front: What does the subcutaneous tissue do?
flashcards.back: Stores about half of the body's fat, insulates and cushions, and anchors skin to underlying structures. It is not technically skin.

flashcards.front: Where do you assess pallor, cyanosis, and jaundice in a client with dark skin?
flashcards.back: Pallor: looks yellow-brown or ashen gray. Cyanosis: nail beds, lips, buccal mucosa. Jaundice: palms and soles, not just the sclera.

flashcards.front: How do you detect inflammation or early pressure damage in darker skin?
flashcards.back: Look for darker, taut, shiny, or indurated areas. Check temperature, edema, and induration. Moistening the skin may help reveal changes.

flashcards.front: Primary vs secondary lesion?
flashcards.back: Primary arises from normal skin (macule, papule, nodule, vesicle, pustule, bulla, wheal). Secondary develops from a primary lesion or trauma (crust, scale, scar, keloid, fissure, ulcer, erosion).

flashcards.front: Acute vs chronic skin disorders?
flashcards.back: Acute: short-term, situational (bacterial infection, dermatitis); reduce inflammation, avoid triggers. Chronic: long-term or lifelong; treatment = remission, not cure.

flashcards.front: Give an example of each type of infectious skin disorder.
flashcards.back: Bacterial → impetigo. Fungal → athlete's foot. Viral → chickenpox. Parasitic → lice.

flashcards.front: Honey-colored crusts around a child's nose and mouth?
flashcards.back: Impetigo (bacterial). Contact precautions, gently wash crusts off, give the prescribed antibiotic, don't share towels, and keep nails short.

flashcards.front: Isolation for chickenpox?
flashcards.back: Airborne + contact until all lesions are crusted. Assign only staff with documented immunity. No aspirin for children (Reye syndrome).

flashcards.front: Which clients are most endangered by fungal skin infections?
flashcards.back: Immunocompromised clients (for example, those receiving chemotherapy or with HIV/AIDS).

flashcards.front: Allergic vs irritant contact dermatitis?
flashcards.back: Allergic: immune reaction at the allergen site, shaped like the item, with vesicles or wheals; mostly adults; patch test. Irritant: chemicals, soap, detergent; not immune-related; strongest in infants.

flashcards.front: Classic psoriasis lesion and treatment goal?
flashcards.back: Well-defined red plaques with silvery-white scale on the elbows, knees, and scalp. It is chronic, so the goal is remission, not cure.

flashcards.front: Bathing and skin care for eczema?
flashcards.back: Short lukewarm bath, mild fragrance-free cleanser, pat dry and moisturize right away. Avoid wool, fragrance, and heat.

flashcards.front: Name the three neoplastic skin disorders. Which is most serious?
flashcards.back: Basal cell carcinoma (most common), squamous cell carcinoma, and malignant melanoma (most serious).

flashcards.front: ABCDE of melanoma?
flashcards.back: Asymmetry, Border irregular, Color variation, Diameter larger than about 6 mm, Evolving (any change).

flashcards.front: Where should a skin self-exam focus?
flashcards.back: Sun-exposed areas (face, neck, ears, scalp, arms, legs), plus the trunk, chest, and feet.

flashcards.front: Key preventive measures for skin disorders?
flashcards.back: Sun protection (sunscreen, hats, protective clothing), proper hygiene and skin care, keep skin clean, dry, and moisturized, avoid irritants and allergens, and don't share personal items.

flashcards.front: The 4 wound classes by contamination?
flashcards.back: Clean (no tract entered, sterile), Clean-contaminated (controlled entry into GI, GU, or respiratory tract), Contaminated (open, fresh, major sterile break, spillage), Dirty/Infected (pus, dead tissue, clinical infection).

flashcards.front: Intentional vs unintentional? Closed vs open?
flashcards.back: Intentional: created for therapy (surgery, venipuncture). Unintentional: accidental. Closed: skin intact, tissue injured (contusion). Open: skin or mucous membrane broken.

flashcards.front: Partial vs full-thickness healing?
flashcards.back: Partial (epidermis and part of dermis) heals by regeneration. Full (all skin layers, may reach muscle or bone) needs connective tissue repair.

flashcards.front: Acute care for an untreated wound?
flashcards.back: Pressure and elevate to control bleeding → clean with saline and cover → ice for pain and swelling → assess for shock (rapid pulse, clammy skin, low BP).

flashcards.front: Albumin value that signals risk for delayed healing?
flashcards.back: Less than 3.5 g/dL: poor nutrition, ↑ infection risk, delayed healing.

flashcards.front: KOH prep, Tzanck test, patch test, biopsy: what does each detect?
flashcards.back: KOH: fungus. Tzanck: viral lesions. Patch test: contact allergy. Biopsy: benign vs cancerous.

flashcards.front: How do WBC, hemoglobin, and coagulation results affect healing?
flashcards.back: ↓ WBC: poor infection defense. ↓ Hemoglobin: less oxygen to tissue. Prolonged clotting: bleeding; hypercoagulability: clotting and poor perfusion.

flashcards.front: Nutrients that support tissue repair?
flashcards.back: ↑ Calories and protein, vitamins A and C. Whole grains, vegetables, citrus, dairy, lean proteins; small frequent meals or supplements if needed.

flashcards.front: Benzoyl peroxide vs salicylic acid?
flashcards.back: Benzoyl peroxide: first-line acne treatment; kills bacteria and unplugs ducts. Salicylic acid: exfoliates and reduces inflammation.

flashcards.front: How to apply a topical corticosteroid?
flashcards.back: Thin layer with gloves, no occlusion unless ordered, avoid stronger products on the face and skin folds. Long-term use can thin the skin.

flashcards.front: Complementary skin therapies and the nurse's role?
flashcards.back: Aloe vera, chamomile, evening primrose oil may soothe irritation, but evidence is limited. Ask about use and monitor for drug interactions and allergies.

flashcards.front: Expected newborn skin findings?
flashcards.back: Vernix caseosa, milia, neonatal acne, erythema toxicum, and birthmarks. Thin skin → heat loss and ↑ absorption.

flashcards.front: Intrinsic vs extrinsic aging?
flashcards.back: Intrinsic: natural, starts about age 20 (↓ moisture, ↓ fat, ↓ collagen in the 40s, thinner after menopause). Extrinsic: UV, pollution, smoking, chemicals → thickening, precancerous changes, wrinkles.

flashcards.front: Why bathe older adults every other day with lukewarm water?
flashcards.back: ↓ Sebaceous glands → dry, fragile skin. Frequent hot bathing strips oils and causes dryness, itching, and skin tears.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Skin Structure & Function
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.hintContent: Recall which skin layer contains blood vessels and nerve endings, and what is left behind in a wound that goes only partway through the skin.
questions.hintStrategy: Use two clues from the stem: the wound bleeds, and no fat is visible. Eliminate any option that contradicts either clue.
questions.stem: A client fell from a bicycle and has a scraped knee that is oozing small drops of blood and is painful to touch. No fat or deeper tissue is visible in the wound bed. Which statement by the nurse best describes this wound and how it will heal?
options: It is limited to the epidermis, which has capillaries, so it will heal with a flat scar.
It is full thickness because it bleeds, so it will fill in with connective tissue and scar.
It reaches the dermis and is partial thickness, so it should regrow the same tissue.
It extends into the subcutaneous fat, so it will need surgical closure to heal.
optionRationales: Incorrect. The epidermis is avascular. A wound confined to it would not bleed, and an epidermal wound heals without a scar.
Incorrect. Bleeding means the dermis has been reached, not that all layers are lost. No fat or deeper tissue is visible, so it is not full thickness.

Correct. Bleeding and pain mean the injury reached the dermis, where vessels and nerve endings live. Skin cells left in the follicles and glands of the dermis let a partial-thickness wound heal by regeneration.
Incorrect. No fat is visible, so the wound has not reached the subcutaneous tissue, and a scrape like this does not need surgical closure.
questions.rationale: The epidermis has no blood vessels and few pain endings, so bleeding plus pain places the injury in the dermis. A wound through the epidermis into part of the dermis is partial thickness. Because hair follicles and glands in the remaining dermis still hold living skin cells, it heals by regeneration with little or no scar. Full-thickness wounds lose all skin layers and must fill in with connective tissue (scar).
questions.takeaway: Bleeds and hurts = dermis reached; partial thickness = regeneration, little or no scar.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Skin Structure & Function
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.hintContent: Think about what the skin barrier holds in and keeps out, and how a child's body surface area compares with an adult's.
questions.hintStrategy: Use Maslow: an immediate physiological threat comes before psychosocial or long-term developmental concerns.
questions.stem: A 3-year-old is admitted after a scald injury that removed the epidermis and dermis over a large area of the back and legs. Considering the functions of the skin and the child's age, which concern is the nurse's priority?
options: Disturbed body image because the injured areas will be visible to other children
Reduced vitamin D synthesis because less skin is available for UV exposure
Fluid loss and infection because the barrier is gone over a large surface area
Delayed growth and development because the child will be in the hospital for weeks
optionRationales: Incorrect. Body image matters, but it is a psychosocial concern and does not threaten the child's life right now.
Incorrect. Vitamin D synthesis is a real skin function, but loss of it is a slow, long-term problem, not an immediate threat.

Correct. The barrier that keeps fluid in and germs out is gone. Children have a larger body surface area for their weight, so they lose fluid and heat faster than adults. This is the immediate physical threat.
Incorrect. Development is a valid long-term concern, but it is not as urgent as fluid loss and infection.
questions.rationale: Losing the epidermis and dermis removes the skin's protective barrier, so fluid escapes and microorganisms enter. A young child has more skin surface compared with body weight, so the same injury causes proportionally greater fluid and heat loss. Physiological threats such as fluid volume and infection come before psychosocial, developmental, or long-term concerns.
questions.takeaway: Large skin loss threatens fluid, infection, and heat, and children lose fluid faster because of their larger body surface area.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Skin Structure & Function
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.hintContent: Recall the three jobs of the subcutaneous tissue (insulate, cushion, anchor) and where older adults lose fat.
questions.hintStrategy: Several options are real aging changes. For each one, ask which structure causes it, and keep only those caused by the fat layer.
questions.stem: An 84-year-old client in a long-term care facility has the findings below. Which findings are best explained by the age-related loss of subcutaneous tissue? Select all that apply.
options: Reports feeling cold in a 22 °C (72 °F) room and asks for extra blankets
Did not notice a burn from a heating pad left on the lower back
Has very dry, flaky, itchy skin on the shins
Skin appears paler and more translucent than in earlier photos
Has little cushioning over the sacrum and heels
Has hollowed cheeks and thin, bony-looking hands
optionRationales: Correct. Subcutaneous fat insulates the body. With less of it, the older adult loses heat and feels cold easily.
Incorrect. Not noticing a burn reflects decreased sensation from fewer or less sensitive nerve endings, not loss of fat.
Incorrect. Dry, itchy skin comes from fewer sebaceous (oil) glands in the dermis.
Incorrect. Paler, translucent skin comes from fewer melanocytes and a thinner dermis.
Correct. Subcutaneous fat cushions bony areas. Less padding over the sacrum and heels also raises the risk for pressure injury.
Correct. Older adults lose fat from the face and hands (and gain it in the thighs and abdomen), which explains hollow cheeks and bony hands.
questions.rationale: The subcutaneous tissue stores about half of the body's fat, which insulates, cushions, and anchors the skin. In older adults this layer shrinks, especially in the face and hands, so the client feels cold, looks thinner in the face and hands, and has less padding over bony prominences, a key reason older adults are at higher risk for pressure injuries. Reduced sensation, dry skin, and pale skin are aging changes too, but they come from the nerves, oil glands, and melanocytes.
questions.takeaway: Less subcutaneous fat means less insulation and less padding over bony prominences.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.hintContent: Recall where melanin is lowest and where color changes show up best in darker skin.
questions.hintStrategy: Eliminate options that inspect heavily pigmented skin. Choose the site with the least pigment.
questions.stem: A client with deeply pigmented skin and a COPD exacerbation has an SpO₂ of 86% on 2 L/min by nasal cannula and is increasingly short of breath. The nurse wants to assess for central cyanosis. Which area should the nurse inspect?
options: The skin of the forehead and cheeks
The skin over the sternum
The dorsal surface of the hands
The lips and buccal (oral) mucosa
optionRationales: Incorrect. Facial skin in a deeply pigmented client may hide the gray or blue tint of cyanosis.
Incorrect. The skin over the sternum is pigmented and is not a reliable place to see cyanosis in dark skin.
Incorrect. The backs of the hands are pigmented and show peripheral, not central, color change poorly.
Correct. The lips and buccal mucosa have little melanin, so a gray or ashen color from central cyanosis is easiest to see there.
questions.rationale: Melanin can mask color changes in darker skin. Cyanosis in dark skin often appears gray or ashen rather than blue, so the nurse inspects areas with little pigment: the lips, buccal mucosa, and nail beds. The mucous membranes of the mouth are the best place to judge central cyanosis.
questions.takeaway: In dark skin, look for cyanosis in the lips, buccal mucosa, and nail beds.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Skin Assessment & Lesions
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.hintContent: Recall how Stage I looks in darkly pigmented skin and which senses besides sight the nurse can use.
questions.hintStrategy: Judge each technique on its own: would it still work if redness cannot be seen?
questions.stem: A client with dark brown skin has been on bed rest for 3 days. The sacrum looks the same color as the surrounding skin. The nurse wants to find a Stage I pressure injury early. Which assessment techniques should the nurse use? Select all that apply.
options: Palpate the sacrum for warmth or coolness compared with nearby skin
Feel for induration, edema, or a boggy texture over the sacrum
Inspect for skin that is darker, purplish, taut, or shiny
Rely on finding redness that does not fade when pressed
Assess the area in dim light to reduce glare on the skin
Lightly moisten the skin to make color changes easier to see
optionRationales: Correct. Temperature change compared with nearby skin is an early clue of tissue damage that may not be visible in dark skin.
Correct. Firmness, swelling, or bogginess can reveal damage under intact skin even when color looks unchanged.
Correct. In darker skin, Stage I may look darker, purplish, or bluish rather than red, and the skin may be taut or shiny.
Incorrect. Nonblanchable redness is the usual Stage I sign in light skin, but redness may be invisible in dark skin, so the nurse cannot rely on it alone.
Incorrect. Good natural or bright light is needed. Dim light hides color changes.
Correct. Slightly moistening the skin can help reveal subtle color changes.
questions.rationale: Stage I is intact skin with nonblanchable erythema, but in darkly pigmented skin it may appear as darkening (purple or bluish tones) or show no visible change. The nurse therefore combines inspection in good light (darker, taut, or shiny areas, with moistening if needed) with palpation for warmth or coolness, edema, and induration compared with surrounding skin.
questions.takeaway: In dark skin, feel for warmth, edema, and firmness and look for darkening; do not wait to see redness.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Skin Assessment & Lesions
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.hintContent: Recall how pallor looks in dark skin and the signs of shock after a wound or surgery.
questions.hintStrategy: Connect the abnormal vital signs to one skin finding. Chronic or harmless findings are distractors.
questions.stem: Four hours after abdominal surgery, a client with dark skin is restless. Vital signs: HR 122/min, BP 92/58 mm Hg, RR 24/min, SpO₂ 93%. Which assessment finding requires the most immediate follow-up?
options: Hyperpigmented macules on the forearms from a previous rash
Ashen-gray lips and oral mucosa with cool, clammy skin
Dry, flaking skin on both lower legs and feet
A 2-cm keloid on the right earlobe from an old piercing
optionRationales: Incorrect. Dark marks after a healed rash are common in darker skin and are not urgent.
Correct. In dark skin, pallor appears ashen gray in the lips and mucosa. With cool, clammy skin, a rapid pulse, low BP, and restlessness, this suggests shock from bleeding and needs action now.
Incorrect. Dry skin needs a moisturizing plan but is not an immediate threat.
Incorrect. Keloids are more common in darker skin and are not an acute problem.
questions.rationale: In dark skin, pallor looks ashen gray and is best seen in the lips, mucosa, conjunctivae, and nail beds. After surgery, ashen mucosa plus cool, clammy skin, tachycardia, low BP, and restlessness are the classic signs of shock from blood loss. The nurse stays with the client and notifies the provider immediately. The other findings are chronic or expected in darker skin.
questions.takeaway: Ashen gray lips and mucosa in dark skin plus ↑ HR, ↓ BP, and clammy skin = possible shock.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Skin Assessment & Lesions
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.hintContent: Recall the size and content that define a vesicle, bulla, pustule, and wheal, and which infection shows lesions in different stages.
questions.hintStrategy: Check both halves of each option. Both the lesion name and the disease pattern must match the stem.
questions.stem: A 4-year-old with a low-grade fever has an itchy rash on the trunk. The nurse sees red flat spots, raised bumps, clear fluid-filled lesions about 0.5 cm across, and some crusted lesions, all at the same time. Which documentation and interpretation are most accurate?
options: Vesicles in different stages, a pattern typical of chickenpox
Bullae with honey-colored crusts, a pattern typical of impetigo
Pustules on an inflamed base, a pattern typical of acne
Wheals that come and go, a pattern typical of an allergic reaction
optionRationales: Correct. Raised, clear-fluid lesions under 1 cm are vesicles. Lesions in different stages (macules, papules, vesicles, crusts) at the same time are the classic sign of varicella.
Incorrect. Bullae are larger than 1 cm, and impetigo is marked by honey-colored crusts, often around the nose and mouth.
Incorrect. Pustules contain pus, not clear fluid, and acne affects the face of adolescents rather than the trunk of a febrile preschooler.
Incorrect. Wheals are raised, itchy, and irregular but are not fluid-filled and do not crust.
questions.rationale: Lesion vocabulary and disease patterns work together. A raised lesion filled with clear fluid and smaller than 1 cm is a vesicle. Chickenpox comes in crops, so red macules, papules, vesicles, and crusts appear at the same time. Recognizing the pattern lets the nurse document accurately and anticipate airborne and contact precautions.
questions.takeaway: Clear fluid < 1 cm = vesicle; lesions in different stages at once = chickenpox.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Skin Assessment & Lesions
questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.hintContent: Recall the lists of primary and secondary lesions and how each disorder named here changes the skin.
questions.hintStrategy: For each finding, ask: did this appear on normal skin, or did it develop from an earlier lesion?
questions.stem: A 9-year-old is seen in the clinic for several skin complaints. Which findings should the nurse document as primary lesions? Select all that apply.
options: Flat, brown, nonpalpable freckle 4 mm in diameter on the cheek
Dried, honey-colored crust over a lesion on the lip from impetigo
Raised, itchy, irregular hive that appeared after a bee sting
Linear crack in the skin between the toes from athlete's foot
Raised, pus-filled lesion on the chin from acne
Scaly, thickened patch on the elbow from psoriasis
optionRationales: Correct. A flat, nonpalpable color change smaller than 1 cm is a macule, a primary lesion.
Incorrect. A crust is dried serum, blood, or pus that forms after a primary lesion breaks, so it is secondary.
Correct. A hive is a wheal, a primary lesion that appears on normal skin.
Incorrect. A fissure is a crack that develops from dry or infected skin, a secondary lesion.
Correct. A pustule is a primary lesion. In acne it forms when bacteria grow in a plugged follicle.
Incorrect. Scale is flakes of dead epidermis, a secondary change.
questions.rationale: Primary lesions appear first on previously normal skin (macule, papule, nodule, vesicle, bulla, pustule, wheal). Secondary lesions develop from a primary lesion or from trauma or healing (crust, scale, fissure, erosion, ulcer, scar, keloid). Linking each finding to its disorder, such as the crust of impetigo, the fissure of tinea pedis, and the scale of psoriasis, helps the nurse document accurately.
questions.takeaway: Primary = appears first (macule, wheal, pustule); secondary = what it becomes (crust, fissure, scale).

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Skin Assessment & Lesions
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.hintContent: Recall the slide example of a systemic disease that shows up as dry skin and hair loss, and what each skin test looks for.
questions.hintStrategy: Look at the whole cluster of findings, not just the skin. Eliminate tests meant for a single localized lesion.
questions.stem: A 52-year-old client reports dry, rough skin that lotion does not help, thinning hair, brittle nails, weight gain, constipation, and always feeling cold. HR is 56/min. Which test should the nurse anticipate the provider will order?
options: A potassium hydroxide (KOH) preparation of skin scrapings
Thyroid function tests
A patch test on the upper back
A Wood lamp examination of the skin
optionRationales: Incorrect. A KOH prep looks for fungus, which would cause scaly, itchy patches, not these body-wide findings.
Correct. Dry skin and hair loss together with cold intolerance, weight gain, constipation, and a slow pulse point to hypothyroidism, a systemic problem. Thyroid function tests evaluate it.
Incorrect. A patch test identifies a contact allergy, which causes a localized rash.
Incorrect. A Wood lamp helps detect some fungal infections and pigment changes, not a body-wide metabolic problem.
questions.rationale: The skin can reflect systemic disease. The slide example is dry skin plus hair loss pointing to hypothyroidism, and the other findings (cold intolerance, weight gain, constipation, bradycardia) confirm a slowed metabolism. Skin-specific tests such as KOH, patch testing, and Wood lamp answer questions about fungus, allergy, and pigment, so they do not fit this pattern.
questions.takeaway: Dry skin + hair loss + other body-wide signs = think systemic (hypothyroidism), not a skin test.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Infectious Skin Disorders
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
questions.hintContent: Identify the infection from the lesion description, then recall how it spreads and how its crusts are treated.
questions.hintStrategy: This asks for a CORRECT statement. Eliminate any statement that would spread the infection or block treatment.
questions.stem: A 5-year-old has small blisters around the nose and mouth that have broken open and formed honey-colored crusts. An antibiotic ointment is prescribed. Which statement by the parent indicates the teaching was effective?
options: “She can go back to kindergarten tomorrow morning since the ointment started tonight.”
“I'll cover the sores tightly with plastic wrap at night so they heal faster.”
“The whole family can keep sharing towels as long as we wash them weekly.”
“I'll gently wash off the crusts and dry the area before putting on the ointment.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. A child with impetigo stays home until 24 hours after effective treatment starts.
Incorrect. Occlusive plastic wrap traps moisture and is not part of impetigo care.
Incorrect. Impetigo spreads by direct contact and shared items. Each person needs their own towel.
Correct. The honey-colored crusts are a secondary lesion typical of impetigo. Gently washing them off and drying the skin lets the ointment reach the infection.
questions.rationale: Vesicles that rupture and leave honey-colored crusts around the nose and mouth are the hallmark of impetigo, a contagious bacterial infection. Care includes gently washing off crusts, patting dry, and applying the prescribed ointment; using separate towels; keeping nails short; and staying home until 24 hours of effective treatment.
questions.takeaway: Impetigo: wash off the honey crusts, apply ointment, no sharing, home until 24 hours of treatment.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Skin Cancer, Screening & Prevention
questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.hintContent: Recall how diabetes and obesity raise skin risk and which conditions let fungi and bacteria grow.
questions.hintStrategy: Judge each option as true or false. Watch for options that sound protective but dry the skin or spread germs.
questions.stem: A 52-year-old client with type 2 diabetes and obesity asks how to keep the skin healthy and prevent infections. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options: Keep the skin clean and dry, especially in skin folds and between the toes
Apply a moisturizer regularly, such as right after bathing
Scrub the skin with antibacterial soap several times a day
Cover any cut or scrape and watch it for redness, swelling, or drainage
Choose fragrance-free and dye-free soaps and laundry products
Share towels only with family members who live in the same home
optionRationales: Correct. Moisture trapped in skin folds and between the toes lets fungus and bacteria grow, a particular risk with diabetes and obesity.
Correct. Moisturizing keeps the skin from cracking, which would open a door for germs.
Incorrect. Excessive cleansing strips natural oils and dries the skin, which increases the risk of breakdown.
Correct. Covering wounds reduces infection risk, and the client should know the signs of infection to report.
Correct. Avoiding dyes and perfumes reduces irritant and allergic reactions.
Incorrect. Sharing towels spreads fungi, bacteria, and lice, even within a household.
questions.rationale: Chronic illnesses such as diabetes and obesity are modifiable risk factors that weaken skin defenses: high glucose feeds bacteria, circulation is poorer, and skin folds trap moisture where fungi (tinea) thrive. Teaching focuses on keeping skin clean, dry, and moisturized, covering wounds, avoiding irritants, and not sharing personal items, while avoiding over-washing.
questions.takeaway: Clean, dry, moisturized, covered, and not shared; over-washing is the wrong answer.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Diagnostics, Labs & Nursing Care
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.hintContent: Recall which organism causes recurring clusters of painful lip vesicles, and which test looks for that organism.
questions.hintStrategy: Work in two steps: identify the likely cause from the lesion pattern, then match that cause to a test.
questions.stem: A client has a painful cluster of small, clear, fluid-filled lesions on a red base at the border of the upper lip. The client says, “I get these every time I'm stressed.” Which diagnostic test should the nurse anticipate?
options: Tzanck test of cells from the base of a vesicle
Patch testing on the upper back
Potassium hydroxide (KOH) preparation of skin scrapings
Wood lamp examination in a darkened room
optionRationales: Correct. Painful clustered vesicles on the lip that recur with stress suggest herpes simplex. A Tzanck test looks for changes caused by herpes-type viruses.
Incorrect. A patch test detects contact allergy. A contact allergy rash takes the shape of the item that touched the skin.
Incorrect. A KOH prep detects fungus, which causes scaly, itchy patches rather than painful clustered vesicles.
Incorrect. A Wood lamp helps detect some fungal infections and pigment changes.
questions.rationale: The lesions are vesicles (clear fluid, under 1 cm) in a painful cluster on the lip that recur with stress, the typical pattern of herpes simplex (cold sores). A Tzanck test examines cells scraped from the base of a fresh vesicle for changes caused by herpes-family viruses. Matching the lesion pattern to the likely organism, and the organism to the test, is the key skill.
questions.takeaway: Painful clustered vesicles on the lip → herpes → Tzanck test.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Infectious Skin Disorders
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
questions.hintContent: Identify the infection from the lesion pattern, then recall how it spreads and who is at risk from exposure.
questions.hintStrategy: Ask which staff member is protected from the infection. Eliminate anyone who is at risk or whose immunity is unknown.
questions.stem: A febrile 6-year-old is admitted with crops of itchy lesions on the trunk and face, including red macules, papules, clear vesicles, and crusts at the same time. The child is placed in an airborne infection isolation room. Which staff member is most appropriate to assign to this child?
options: An RN who is 14 weeks pregnant and unsure of her chickenpox history
An RN who recently finished chemotherapy for breast cancer
An RN who had chickenpox as a child and has documented immunity
A float LPN who has never had chickenpox or the varicella vaccine
optionRationales: Incorrect. Varicella can harm a pregnancy, and her immunity is not confirmed.
Incorrect. A nurse recovering from chemotherapy may be immunocompromised and at risk for severe infection.
Correct. Lesions in several stages at once indicate chickenpox, which spreads through the air and by contact. Only staff with documented immunity should care for the child.
Incorrect. A nonimmune staff member is at high risk of catching varicella.
questions.rationale: Crops of lesions in different stages (macules, papules, vesicles, crusts) at the same time are the hallmark of varicella. It is highly contagious by airborne and contact routes until all lesions crust, so the child needs airborne plus contact precautions, and only staff with documented immunity (past infection or vaccination) should be assigned. Pregnant, immunocompromised, and nonimmune staff should not be.
questions.takeaway: Chickenpox: airborne + contact precautions and immune staff only, never pregnant or nonimmune staff.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Diagnostics, Labs & Nursing Care
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
questions.hintContent: Recall the steps of gentle bathing for older skin and which aging change makes hot water dangerous.
questions.hintStrategy: All options are correct steps. Put them in order and pick the one that must come before the skin touches the water.
questions.stem: The nurse is helping an 82-year-old client with thin, dry skin and decreased sensation in the feet take a bath. After performing hand hygiene, which action should the nurse take first?
options: Wash the skin gently with a mild liquid cleanser
Apply a moisturizer to the driest areas of the skin
Check that the bath water is lukewarm
Pat the skin dry with a soft towel
optionRationales: Incorrect. Gentle washing with a mild cleanser is correct, but it comes after the water temperature is checked.
Incorrect. Moisturizer is applied after bathing, while the skin is still slightly damp.
Correct. The client has decreased sensation and may not feel water that is too hot. Hot water also dries thin skin. Checking that the water is lukewarm protects the client before the skin touches it.
Incorrect. Patting dry is correct, but it comes near the end of the bath.
questions.rationale: Older adults have thinner skin, fewer oil glands, and decreased sensation, so hot water can both dry the skin and burn a client who cannot feel it. The nurse checks for lukewarm water first, then washes gently with a mild cleanser, rinses, pats dry, and moisturizes while the skin is slightly damp. Per the slides, older adults bathe every other day.
questions.takeaway: Older skin: check lukewarm water first, then mild cleanser, pat dry, and moisturize.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Infectious Skin Disorders
questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.hintContent: Recall how an OTC pediculicide is used correctly and how lice spread through shared items.
questions.hintStrategy: Judge each instruction on its own. Watch for steps that block the medicine or add risk without benefit.
questions.stem: The school nurse is teaching the parents of a 7-year-old who has head lice and will be treated with an over-the-counter (OTC) pediculicide shampoo. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options: Use a fine-tooth nit comb to remove nits from the hair
Wash recently used bedding and hats in hot water and dry them on high heat
Use a conditioner right before applying the lice shampoo
Spray the furniture and carpets with an insecticide fogger
Tell your child not to share combs, brushes, or hats
Recheck the hair in about a week, since a second treatment is often needed
optionRationales: Correct. Nits are glued to the hair shaft and must be combed out.
Correct. Hot washing and high-heat drying kill lice and nits on recently used items.
Incorrect. Conditioner coats the hair and keeps the pediculicide from working.
Incorrect. Foggers and insecticide sprays are not needed and can be harmful. Vacuuming is enough.
Correct. Lice spread through head-to-head contact and shared items.
Correct. Rechecking finds newly hatched lice, and a second treatment is often needed.
questions.rationale: Minor lice cases are treated with an OTC pediculicide, and OTC products still require careful teaching: follow the label exactly and do not use conditioner first. Nits must be combed out, recently used items washed hot and dried on high heat (or bagged for about 2 weeks), personal items not shared, and the hair rechecked in about a week. Foggers are unnecessary and potentially harmful.
questions.takeaway: Lice: follow the label, no conditioner first, comb nits, hot wash, no sharing, recheck in a week.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Diagnostics, Labs & Nursing Care
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.hintContent: Recall what a ring-shaped scaly patch with central clearing suggests and which test detects that organism.
questions.hintStrategy: First name the likely organism (fungus, virus, allergy, bacteria), then match it to the test that finds it.
questions.stem: A 16-year-old wrestler has a 3-cm itchy, scaly, ring-shaped patch with a raised border and a clearer center on the forearm. Two teammates have similar lesions. Which diagnostic test should the nurse anticipate to confirm the most likely cause?
options: Tzanck test of cells from the lesion base
KOH preparation of lesion scrapings
Patch testing on the upper back
Nasal culture for Staphylococcus aureus
optionRationales: Incorrect. A Tzanck test looks for herpes-type viruses, which cause clustered vesicles, not a scaly ring.
Correct. A scaly ring with central clearing that spreads among teammates suggests tinea corporis (ringworm). A KOH prep shows fungal threads in scrapings from the lesion edge.
Incorrect. A patch test identifies a contact allergy, which would not spread from person to person.
Incorrect. A nasal carrier culture is used for repeated staph infections such as boils.
questions.rationale: Ringworm (tinea corporis) is a fungal infection that forms a round, scaly patch spreading outward with a clearer center. It spreads by skin contact and shared items, which fits a wrestling team. A KOH prep dissolves skin cells so fungus can be seen under a microscope, confirming the cause.
questions.takeaway: Scaly ring with a clear center → tinea → KOH prep.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.hintContent: Recall what makes a rash take the exact shape of an object, and which test detects a delayed contact allergy.
questions.hintStrategy: Each option has a diagnosis and a test. Both parts must be correct.
questions.stem: A client reports an itchy, red rash with small vesicles on the left wrist that is exactly the shape of the metal watch band she has worn for years. Which interpretation and follow-up are most accurate?
options: Allergic contact dermatitis to a metal such as nickel; a patch test can confirm it
Tinea corporis from fungus living on the band; a Wood lamp exam will confirm it
Irritant contact dermatitis from soap trapped under the band; a KOH prep will confirm it
Atopic dermatitis triggered by her history of asthma; a skin biopsy will confirm it
optionRationales: Correct. A vesicular rash shaped exactly like the object, after years of exposure (sensitization), is a delayed allergic reaction. Metals such as nickel are common causes, and a patch test identifies the allergen.
Incorrect. Tinea forms a scaly ring with central clearing, not vesicles shaped like an object.
Incorrect. Irritant dermatitis causes red, dry, cracked skin without an object's exact shape, and a KOH prep detects fungus, not irritation.
Incorrect. Atopic dermatitis appears in skin creases and is not shaped like an object, and a biopsy is used to tell benign from cancerous lesions.
questions.rationale: Allergic contact dermatitis is an immune reaction that requires prior sensitization and appears where the allergen touched the skin, often shaped like the item (watch band, ring, glove edge). Years of wearing the watch allowed sensitization. The patch test is the test for contact (delayed) allergy.
questions.takeaway: Rash shaped like the object = allergic contact dermatitis; confirm with a patch test.

questions.hintContent: Recall the pattern of allergic contact dermatitis, the test that confirms it, and how topical steroids are applied.

questions.stem: A dental assistant has itchy, red skin with small vesicles on both hands and wrists that ends in a sharp line where her gloves stop. It began about 2 days after she started using a new brand of latex gloves. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.
options: Document the suspected latex allergy in the client's record
Use nonlatex gloves and supplies when caring for the client
Teach the client to switch to a stronger antibacterial soap at work
Explain that patch testing can confirm the allergen
Apply the prescribed topical corticosteroid in a thin layer
Tell the client the reaction will lessen as her skin gets used to latex
optionRationales: Correct. Documenting the allergy protects the client in all future care.
Correct. The client must avoid the allergen, including in the nurse's own care.
Incorrect. Harsh soap irritates skin and does not treat an allergy.
Correct. The patch test is used to confirm a contact (delayed) allergy.
Correct. A thin layer of topical corticosteroid reduces inflammation and itching.
Incorrect. Allergic reactions tend to stay the same or worsen with repeated exposure.
questions.rationale: A rash shaped like the gloves that began 2 days after a new exposure is allergic contact dermatitis, a delayed immune reaction. Care connects three ideas: remove and document the allergen (latex), confirm it with a patch test, and calm the inflammation with a thin layer of prescribed topical corticosteroid. Harsh soap and continued exposure make it worse.
questions.takeaway: Allergic contact dermatitis: document, avoid the allergen, patch test, thin layer of steroid.

questions.hintContent: Recall what is wrong with the skin barrier in eczema and what a moisturizer does for it.
questions.hintStrategy: Eliminate options that dry or irritate the skin. The best answer repairs the barrier.
questions.stem: The parent of a 4-year-old with atopic dermatitis (eczema) in the creases of the elbows and knees asks about bath time. Which instruction is most important for the nurse to include?
options: Give a long, hot bath each evening with a scented bubble bath
Rub the skin briskly with a towel after bathing to remove loose scales
Dress the child in wool clothing in winter to keep the skin warm
Pat dry and apply a thick, fragrance-free moisturizer right away
optionRationales: Incorrect. Hot water and fragrance dry and irritate eczema-prone skin.
Incorrect. Rubbing damages the fragile barrier and worsens the itch–scratch cycle.
Incorrect. Wool is scratchy and triggers itching. Soft cotton is preferred.
Correct. Eczema is caused by a weak skin barrier that loses water. Patting dry and sealing in moisture right away rebuilds the barrier.
questions.rationale: In eczema, the epidermal barrier is weak, so water leaks out and irritants get in, causing dry, itchy skin and the itch–scratch cycle. In older children it typically appears in the antecubital and popliteal creases. The key teaching is a short lukewarm bath with a mild cleanser, patting dry, and applying a thick, fragrance-free moisturizer within minutes to lock in water.
questions.takeaway: Eczema: short lukewarm bath, pat dry, moisturize right away.

questions.hintContent: Recall how chronic skin disorders differ from acute ones in their treatment goal, and how psoriasis is treated.
questions.hintStrategy: Look for the response that is both honest and accurate. Eliminate promises of a cure.
questions.stem: A 34-year-old client newly diagnosed with plaque psoriasis on the elbows and knees asks, “How long will it take for this to be cured?” Which response by the nurse is most accurate?
options: “It should clear for good once you finish a 2-week course of antibiotics.”
“It is long-term, but prescription treatment can keep it in remission.”
“It will go away on its own within a few months, so treatment is optional.”
“Once the scales are scrubbed off, the plaques should not return.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Psoriasis is an immune-related disorder, not an infection, so antibiotics do not cure it.
Correct. Psoriasis is a chronic disorder. The treatment goal is remission, and it is managed with prescription topical or oral medicines.
Incorrect. Psoriasis is chronic and does not resolve on its own.
Incorrect. Scrubbing injures the skin and can trigger a flare. The plaques come from rapid skin-cell buildup.
questions.rationale: Psoriasis is a chronic, immune-related disorder in which skin cells build up in days instead of weeks, forming silvery plaques. Chronic skin disorders are classified by their long course, and their goal is remission, not cure. Unlike minor acne or lice, psoriasis is treated with prescription medicines. The nurse's answer should be honest and hopeful.
questions.takeaway: Chronic skin disorder (psoriasis) = remission, not cure; prescription treatment.

questions.stem: A newly hired nurse aide washes her hands with soap and water 40 to 50 times per shift. Within her first week she developed dry, red, cracked, burning skin across the backs of both hands, with no distinct shape. Which recommendations should the nurse make? Select all that apply.
options: Use alcohol-based hand rub when the hands are not visibly soiled
Apply a facility-approved moisturizer often during and after each shift
Rinse the hands with hot water to remove all soap residue
Wear latex gloves for all tasks to protect the skin
Skip hand hygiene between clients until the skin heals
Use lukewarm water and pat the hands dry instead of rubbing
optionRationales: Correct. Alcohol-based rub is gentler than repeated soap and water and still meets hand hygiene requirements.
Correct. Moisturizer repairs the damaged skin barrier.
Incorrect. Hot water strips oils and worsens dryness and cracking.
Incorrect. Constant glove use traps moisture, and latex can cause a new allergy.
Incorrect. Hand hygiene before and after client care must continue to prevent spreading infection.
Correct. Lukewarm water and patting dry reduce further damage to the skin.
questions.rationale: Red, dry, cracked, burning skin from frequent washing, with no object shape and no delay, is irritant contact dermatitis: direct damage from soap, not an immune reaction. The aide must keep performing hand hygiene, since it prevents infection, so the plan protects the skin while doing it: use alcohol-based rub when hands are not visibly soiled, lukewarm water, pat dry, and moisturize often.
questions.takeaway: Irritant hand dermatitis: keep doing hand hygiene, but use hand rub, lukewarm water, and moisturizer.

questions.hintContent: Recall how skin tone affects skin cancer risk and where melanoma is often found in darker skin.
questions.hintStrategy: Eliminate responses that use absolute words (only, can't, always) about who or where skin cancer occurs.
questions.stem: A 34-year-old client with dark brown skin asks how to do a monthly skin self-examination. Which response by the nurse is most accurate?
options: “Check sun-exposed areas and your trunk, and include your palms, soles, and nails.”
“Focus on your face and hands, because skin cancer forms only where the sun hits.”
“Because you have dark skin, you can't get skin cancer, so a yearly check is enough.”
“Check only the spots that itch or hurt, since skin cancer always causes symptoms first.”
optionRationales: Correct. Self-exams cover sun-exposed areas plus the trunk, chest, and feet. In darker skin, melanoma is more often found on the palms, soles, and under the nails.
Incorrect. Skin cancer can form in areas with little sun exposure, including the soles and nail beds.
Incorrect. All skin tones are at risk. In darker skin, cancer is often found later, so self-exams matter.
Incorrect. Skin cancer often causes no symptoms early. Changes in appearance are what matter.
questions.rationale: Melanin gives some UV protection, but no skin tone is immune to skin cancer, and in darker skin it is often found later and in low-sun areas such as the palms, soles, and nails. A complete self-exam covers sun-exposed areas (face, neck, ears, scalp, arms, legs) plus the trunk, chest, and feet, including soles and nails.
questions.takeaway: Every skin tone needs self-exams, and dark skin needs extra attention to the palms, soles, and nails.
